### Introducing the Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin: scaling design-driven AI software development

#### Thursday, October 22, 2026

by Brian Suchy , Jim Quinn , Elise Ewing , Oliver Newth and Dave Rensin on behalf of the Elephant-Goldfish Model team

## Shifting left in the AI coding era

AI-powered velocity is transformative; however, it has silently introduced a potential reliability crisis by also increasing the velocity of “slop,” bugs, and session context collapse. Generative AI tools excel at increasing coding speed, but pure speed without structured guardrails means we are often auto-scaling our mistakes rather than simply writing code faster. We need a paradigm shift, aligning the human need for system comprehension with AI’s capacity for execution.

As co-author Dave Rensin outlines in the article Elephants, Goldfish, and the New Golden Age of Software Engineering , “Design is the new code.”

## Understanding the Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM)

The EGM framework is a metaphor for a powerful way to develop AI-assisted software quickly and safely with humans intentionally in the loop.

The “Elephant” is a context-rich, long-horizon AI session that holds the end-to-end architectural vision and project memory. No code is written here; it is purely dedicated to design, intent, and capturing micro-decisions. The Elephant session is where the AI interviews you and you debate the merits of your choices.

Conversely, “Goldfish” are stateless, zero-context sessions used strictly to validate specifications. Because they share no “blind spots” with the designer, they act as objective critics, probing for gaps and edge cases.

The goal of this method is for the AI to correctly produce the code you wanted the first time after you press Enter.

## Announcing the open source Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin

To put this methodology into practice at scale, we are thrilled to announce the Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin . Originally, this plugin was developed internally for Google software engineers, and is now open source. Thousands of Googlers use this plugin every day to ship production Google code. Released under the Apache 2.0 license, the repository provides everything you need to implement this framework. Developers will find customizable Markdown rules, defined subagent personas, and structured review workflows ready to integrate into your own environments.

The plugin’s core goal is to bring the EGM framework directly into Antigravity, with other development environments upcoming. It automates the orchestration of the EGM lifecycle: managing context transfer between Elephants and Goldfish, facilitating validation loops, and rendering design documents, shifting the developer’s role from micromanager to executive reviewer.

## The EGM plugin in a nutshell

The EGM lifecycle, automated with the plugin, walks the user through three co-design phases:

### Phase 1: Growing the Elephant ( egm-brainstorm )

Developers load the system context and adhere to a “No Code” rule to co-design features, debate trade-offs, and challenge assumptions.

### Phase 2: Drafting with the Elephant ( egm-draft )

Developers iteratively draft a Markdown design document that covers the problem definition, technical plan, alternatives considered, and a detailed implementation plan that enumerates the specific files to change.

### Phase 3: The Goldfish Protocol ( egm-review )

The Goldfish Protocol shifts the model from co-design to adversarial validation, using stateless AI instances to probe the design for weaknesses. The plugin automates a three-step validation sequence:

- Comprehension Check: A stateless Goldfish reads the complete design document and must explain the architecture and intent back to the Elephant. If the Goldfish cannot accurately summarize the plan, it indicates the document is ambiguous and requires further drafting.

- Antagonistic Review: Multiple Goldfish instances assume the role of skeptical, antagonistic technical reviewers. They are tasked with identifying potential edge cases, hidden dependencies, and logical gaps. Their critique is funneled back to the Elephant session for resolution.

- Implementation Readiness Check: A final Goldfish performs a strict go/no-go check. It verifies that all necessary information—file paths, data structures, and function signatures—is present and unambiguous. This ensures the spec is ready for precise transcription into code.

## Human judgment is the artifact

Ultimately, human judgment is the only artifact that truly matters in an AI-saturated world and we want to align the human need for system comprehension with AI’s capacity for execution. We hope this plugin will make it easier for developers of all skill levels to follow a process that more quickly and safely converts the idea they had in their head to a robust and well-built app on their screen.

We invite developers, architects, and AI enthusiasts to contribute to the plugin, customize its validation rules, and help define the future of collaborative software engineering.

To get started, check out the Elephant-Goldfish Model repository on GitHub .

### Sandboxing Untrusted AI Agents at Scale: Google Donates Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF

#### Thursday, November 5, 2026

by Mofi Rahman , Developer Relations Engineer, and Brandon Royal , Product Manager, Google Cloud

When Google introduced Kubernetes twelve years ago, the Pod became the default unit of compute for the cloud. The design assumed a straightforward lifecycle: a program boots, binds to a port, serves traffic, and runs until you stop it.

AI agents work fundamentally differently.

An AI agent that’s running on a machine executes untrusted code, commands, and tool calls, and must be isolated from its host and its network resources. At the same time, these agents, whether they’re an interactive coding assistant, an SRE troubleshooter, or a multi-turn evaluation loop, do not run continuously. They execute a step, call a language model, and wait. Most of the time, the agent does nothing at all while it waits for a model to stream tokens or a human to review a pull request. In the same way that Kubernetes was created to address the needs of containerized applications, we introduced Agent Substrate as a new orchestrator for the emerging agentic applications. Secure by default, highly efficient and built for multi-million agent scale.

Agent Substrate was designed from the ground up for AI agent security and density and brings the best parts of Kubernetes together with a new control and data plane for fully-isolated, ultra-low-latency sandboxed compute and storage. The growing Agent Substrate community has been rapidly building core capabilities and stabilizing APIs, culminating in the latest 1.0 release.

This week at KubeCon North America in Salt Lake City, Google Cloud is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) in Sandbox status, alongside OpenRL.

This post explains why traditional approaches struggle with stateful agents, how Agent Substrate solves the problem, how it connects to enterprise governance on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), and where to see it in action at KubeCon NA 2026.

## Challenges of running AI agents at scale

AI agents introduce two infrastructure bottlenecks that standard Kubernetes was never built to handle: idle resource waste and control plane overload.

### 1. The idle resource problem

During a typical interactive session, an agent can spend 90% to 95% of its time waiting for model inference, external APIs, or human reviews.

During that wait, the agent consumes zero CPU. However, you cannot simply kill the container. The agent holds critical state in memory and on disk: active language runtimes, local Git repositories, uncommitted file edits, and tool sessions.

With standard Kubernetes, platform engineers face two poor options:

- Keep a dedicated Pod running all day: The agent responds quickly because it is already warm, but you pay for idle compute around the clock. At ten thousand active users, cluster costs become unsustainable.

- Scale to zero with serverless containers: You save compute costs while the agent sits idle, but resuming from cold storage forces the container to clone repositories, reinstall packages, and rebuild memory. Wakeup latency climbs past 20 seconds, breaking the interactive experience.

Platform teams need agents that wake up in under 500 milliseconds with full memory and disk state intact—without paying for running Pods while the agent sits idle.

### 2. Control plane overload

The opposite issue occurs when training or evaluating agents. Reinforcement learning loops and benchmark suites need to run untrusted agent code across thousands of tasks at the exact same time.

If every sandbox requires a full Kubernetes Pod, the control plane quickly grinds to a halt. Scheduling, creating, and destroying thousands of short-lived Pods every minute overwhelms etcd, saturates kube-apiserver, and exhausts subnet IP addresses. Kubernetes was built to manage stable application topologies, not to act as a microsecond sandbox allocator.

## How Agent Substrate solves the problem

Agent Substrate adds an actor-based control and data plane built on top of Kubernetes. It solves the idle resource problem by decoupling Actors from Workers:

- Actors hold the state: An Actor represents an individual agent session, complete with its own filesystem, environment variables, memory state, and network rules.

- Workers provide the compute: A Worker is a pre-warmed Kubernetes Pod running in a shared pool (WorkerPool), equipped with container runtimes and sandbox boundaries.

### The lifecycle of an agent turn

- Request parking: An incoming call hits the atenet-router L7 proxy. If the target Actor is suspended, the proxy holds the request in memory and alerts the Substrate controller.

- Fast placement: The controller assigns the Actor to an available slot in the warm Worker pool.

- Sub-second restore: The Actor’s memory and disk state restore from tiered storage, the process wakes up, and the proxy delivers the request. The agent resumes in under 500 milliseconds right where it paused.

- Suspension on idle: When the turn finishes, Substrate snapshots the Actor’s state to tiered storage and frees the Worker slot for other workloads.

Because Substrate manages Actor state directly, thousands of agents can activate, suspend, and resume every second without creating new Pod objects or stressing etcd.

### Safe execution with gVisor and microVMs

Agents frequently execute model-generated, untrusted code. Standard Linux containers share the host kernel, which presents an unacceptable security risk on multi-tenant nodes.

Agent Substrate pairs with gVisor (runsc), Google's open source application kernel written in Go. gVisor intercepts system calls in user space, isolating untrusted code from the host kernel. Because gVisor virtualizes its own memory and process tables, Substrate can freeze a running environment, write memory pages to storage, and restore them on another node in under 500 milliseconds.

For workloads requiring hardware virtualization or custom kernel modules, Substrate also supports Cloud Hypervisor microVMs under the same unified API.

## Why Google donated Agent Substrate to the CNCF

Over the past two years, engineering teams across the industry have run into the same agent scaling boundaries. Without a shared open standard, every organization ends up building custom schedulers on top of VMs or working around Kubernetes.

Donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF gives the cloud-native community a neutral, vendor-independent foundation that works across any conformant Kubernetes cluster.

Together with community projects, they form an open stack for agentic infrastructure:

- Layer 1: Secure Isolation ( gVisor ): Sandboxes untrusted code execution with user-space kernel isolation and fast memory checkpointing.

- Layer 2: Agent Runtime ( Agent Substrate ): Multiplexes stateful actors onto warm worker pools with sub-second wakeups.

- Layer 3: Training Orchestration (OpenRL): Coordinates Kubernetes-native reinforcement learning loops and evaluation sandboxes.
